# How modern AI models work {#sec-ch04}

Words like "deep learning" and "large language model" sound very complex. But they are built from four simple ideas. In this chapter we go through these four ideas, and then see why asking an LLM like ChatGPT to make a decision is not as simple as it looks.

::: {.goals}
- Understand layers, embeddings and attention in simple words.
- See why big models often become overconfident.
- Understand why getting a clean decision out of an LLM is difficult.
:::

## Idea one: layers can draw any shape

One artificial **neuron** is the same as the logistic regression from Chapter 2: it gives each clue some points (its weight), adds them up, and turns the total into a probability. But if you draw the cases on a sheet of paper, one neuron can only divide them with a single straight line.

Some problems need more. For example, activity can be suspicious when it is unusual in *any* direction: an employee who downloads 10,000 files in a day is suspicious, but so is a server that suddenly sends nothing at all. The normal cases sit in the middle, and the suspicious ones surround them on every side. No single straight line can separate the middle from all the edges.

![A toy problem. Blue dots are normal activity; red crosses surround them on every side. One neuron (left) can only draw a straight line through it. With a hidden layer of three neurons (middle) the boundary becomes a triangle; with twelve (right), close to a circle.](/figures/ch06/line-limit.pdf){#fig-line-limit}

The solution is to pass the clues through a layer of neurons first. Each neuron draws its own line, and the next neuron combines these lines. Three lines make a triangle; twelve lines make almost a circle (@fig-line-limit). A network with several such layers is called a **deep** network. Training works the same way as before: predict, measure the mistake, and adjust. To decide how much to change each weight, the mistake is passed backwards through the layers, from the answer to the first layer; this is called **backpropagation** [@rumelhart1986].

The big advantage of deep networks is that they can learn their own clues from raw data like images or text [@lecun2015]. But when we already have clean, useful numbers, a deep network adds little. In our example, a small network does no better than simple logistic regression.

::: {.keyidea}
**Big neural networks are for messy data like photos and text.** When your data is already clean numbers, such as a score or a count, a simple model works almost as well and is much easier to understand.
:::

## Idea two: words as numbers

A computer can only calculate with numbers, so words must become numbers. The trick comes from the study of language: *we understand a word by the words around it.* "Phishing" and "fraud" appear in similar sentences, near words like "email", "link" and "password". If we turn each word into a short list of numbers based on its neighbours, words used in similar ways get similar lists. This list is called an **embedding**. Similar documents also get similar embeddings, and this is how AI search finds related text.

But embeddings capture what a text is *about*, not the exact numbers inside it. To an embedding, an alert with a threat score of 0.05 and one with 0.95 look almost the same. In our example, judging a new alert by looking at past alerts with similar text gives honest probabilities but weak ranking (AUC {{< num ch07 knn.auc f2 >}}, against {{< num ch07 lr.auc f2 >}} for logistic regression).

## Idea three: words that look at each other

"Invoice, not phishing" and "phishing, not invoice" have the same words but opposite meanings. **Attention** solves this. Each word looks at the other words in the sentence and decides which of them change its meaning. In "invoice, not phishing", the word "phishing" pays most attention to "not".


Nobody tells the model about the word "not"; it learns this by itself from examples.

A **transformer** is many attention layers stacked together [@vaswani2017]. There are two types. A **reader** sees the whole input at once, which suits understanding and deciding. A **writer** sees only the words before the current one, because it is producing text one word at a time. LLMs like ChatGPT are writers.

## Idea four: very large models, and a side effect

If we train a huge writer to guess the next word on a huge amount of text, it learns grammar, facts and some reasoning [@kaplan2020]. Then it is tuned with good example answers, and with feedback on which answers people prefer [@ouyang2022]. But people usually prefer answers that sound confident. OpenAI reported that GPT-4's confidence was well calibrated before this tuning and less calibrated after it [@openai2023].


There is a second reason. If a large network is trained for too long, it gets almost every training case right, and then the only way to improve further is to become more and more sure of itself. In the end it is sure about everything. The temperature correction from Chapter 2 helps.

::: {.keyidea}
**Big models are often too sure of themselves.** After long training, they say "99% sure" even when they are often wrong. Always check their numbers on real cases before trusting them.
:::

## How an LLM writes, and why this is a problem for decisions

![The generation loop. The model reads everything so far, produces a probability for every possible next token, one gets picked, it's appended, and the loop runs again.](/figures/ch10/loop.pdf){#fig-loop-06}

An LLM writes one small piece of text at a time, called a **token**: usually a word or part of a word. At each step, it gives a probability to every possible next token, picks one, adds it, and repeats (@fig-loop-06). This creates three problems for decisions.

**Longer answers take more time and money.** Each token waits for the previous one. In our example figures, a one-word answer takes about {{< num ch10 lat_1 f1 >}} seconds, but a long step-by-step answer takes about {{< num ch10 lat_1500 int >}} seconds.

**The same question can get different answers.** The model usually picks the next token with some randomness. In our example, out of forty borderline alerts asked twenty times each, {{< num ch10 n_split int >}} got different answers at different times.

**The answer is hidden inside text.** We can ask the LLM to answer in a fixed, computer-readable format called JSON. Even then, some answers come back broken: with friendly chatting around them, cut off in the middle, or with extra items nobody asked for. Many LLMs offer a "JSON mode" to prevent this. "JSON mode" fixes the *format*, not the *correctness*: a model can still write "benign" for a real attack in perfect format.

![What came back when we asked for JSON, over 4,000 alerts. With only the prompt, some responses were wrapped in friendly chat, some were cut off mid-object, and some were valid JSON with a field nobody asked for. With JSON mode on, the first two problems vanish. The third doesn't.](/figures/ch11/json-failures.pdf){#fig-json-failures}

::: {.keyidea}
**A neatly formatted answer can still be wrong.** An LLM can return a perfect, clean "safe" for a real attack. Checking the format tells you the answer is readable, not that it is right.
:::

## Three kinds of "confidence"

Suppose an LLM replies: `"verdict": "malicious", "confidence": 0.95`. Can we trust this 0.95?


- **The written confidence** is just text that the model wrote. In our example, the LLM used only {{< num ch11 n_distinct_stated int >}} different values, mostly 0.9 or more, so it hardly separates attacks from normal alerts.
- **The token probability** is the probability the model gave to the word "malicious". It ranks better but is overconfident. It is also the probability of one *word*, not of the answer: the same answer can be written as "malicious", "Malicious" or "likely malicious", and the probability gets split among all these spellings.
- **A decision model's probability** is designed to be the probability of the answer itself. Getting such a trustworthy number in one fast step is exactly what System One models are designed for.

::: {.exercises}
1. A company says its classifier is "97% accurate" and gives a confidence with every answer. You plan to act automatically when the confidence is above 0.9. What would you check first?
:::
